academic.title: Academic English Placement
academic.skills: Listening, academic reading, structure and writing
academic.description: Follow a short lecture, interpret research prose and build an evidence-based argument.

Listening to lectures.title: Lecture signposts
Listening to lectures.instruction: Mark phrases such as “first,” “however,” and “to sum up.” Use them to track the speaker’s argument.
Listening to lectures.practice: In “Most seeds sprouted. However, only two survived,” what does “however” signal?
Listening to lectures.answer: A contrast between sprouting and surviving.

Listening to lectures.title: Main claim and supporting evidence
Listening to lectures.instruction: Write the speaker’s claim on one line and any examples or measurements underneath.
Listening to lectures.practice: A speaker says shaded roofs reduce indoor heat, then reports a two-degree difference. Which part is the evidence?
Listening to lectures.answer: The two-degree difference is the measurement that supports the claim.

Listening to lectures.title: Changes to a study plan
Listening to lectures.instruction: Listen for what has changed and what remains scheduled. Take notes under “before” and “after.”
Listening to lectures.practice: A tutor says “We will still meet on Thursday, but bring your draft instead of your bibliography.” What changed?
Listening to lectures.answer: The document to bring. The meeting day stays Thursday.

Academic reading.title: Scope of a result
Academic reading.instruction: Circle words like “some,” “may,” and “among the participants.” They show how far a result applies.
Academic reading.practice: Why does “may improve recall” make a narrower claim than “improves recall”?

Academic reading.title: Method and limitation
Academic reading.instruction: Find how evidence was obtained and one reason it might not apply elsewhere.
Academic reading.practice: A survey includes only people from one campus. Name one limitation.
Academic reading.answer: The sample may not represent students at other campuses.

Academic reading.title: Paraphrasing a finding
Academic reading.instruction: Keep the relationship between ideas and express it in new words.
Academic reading.practice: Paraphrase “The gain disappeared after a week.”
Academic reading.answer: After seven days, the improvement was no longer evident.

Sentence structure.title: Subject and verb agreement
Sentence structure.instruction: Find the head of the subject before choosing a singular or plural verb.
Sentence structure.practice: Choose “is” or “are” in “The list of materials ___ complete.”

Sentence structure.title: Sentence boundaries
Sentence structure.instruction: An independent clause can stand alone. Use a period or suitable connector between independent clauses.
Sentence structure.practice: Fix “The lab was closed, we left.”
Sentence structure.answer: “The lab was closed, so we left.”

Sentence structure.title: Parallel form
Sentence structure.instruction: Items in a list should follow the same grammatical pattern.
Sentence structure.practice: Edit “The team collected, labelled, and was storing samples.”
Sentence structure.answer: “The team collected, labelled, and stored samples.”

Academic writing.title: A qualified thesis
Academic writing.instruction: Take a clear position and name a condition where it applies.
Academic writing.practice: Give a thesis about recording lectures.
Academic writing.answer: “Universities should record large lectures when recordings are accessible to every student.”

Academic writing.title: Evidence and explanation
Academic writing.instruction: Give a specific example, then explain how it supports the claim.
Academic writing.practice: If recordings allow students to replay technical terms, what benefit follows?
Academic writing.answer: Students can review unfamiliar terminology at their own pace.

Academic writing.title: Revising for precision
Academic writing.instruction: Replace broad intensifiers with specific observations.
Academic writing.answer: “The study used the same measurement method in both groups.”

modular.title: Modular Skills Placement
modular.description: Practise the four skills in separate tasks drawn from study and workplace situations.

Reading for a purpose.title: Scan an email
Reading for a purpose.instruction: Scan headings and final lines for deadlines, owners and actions.
Reading for a purpose.practice: In “Please confirm the room by noon Friday,” identify the action and deadline.
Reading for a purpose.answer: Confirm the room by noon Friday.

Reading for a purpose.title: Compare options
Reading for a purpose.instruction: Put each option in a table and compare it against the task constraints.
Reading for a purpose.practice: A room must seat ten. Cedar seats eight; Lotus seats twelve. Which fits?

Reading for a purpose.title: Read implied meaning
Reading for a purpose.instruction: Combine the literal message with context and consider what action the writer expects.
Reading for a purpose.practice: A manager says “We could use another copy before the guests arrive.” What is the likely request?
Reading for a purpose.answer: Print or provide another copy before the guests arrive.

Listening at work and in class.title: Changes in sequence
Listening at work and in class.instruction: Use ordinal words and time expressions to map steps.
Listening at work and in class.practice: In “After checking in, collect a badge before you enter,” what comes between check-in and entry?

Listening at work and in class.title: Speaker purpose
Listening at work and in class.instruction: Identify whether a speaker is informing, persuading, apologizing or requesting action.
Listening at work and in class.practice: What is the purpose of “I’m afraid our booking system is offline. Could you call back after two?”
Listening at work and in class.answer: Explain the interruption and ask the listener to call again.

Listening at work and in class.title: Concessions
Listening at work and in class.instruction: After “although” or “even though,” listen for the decision that follows.
Listening at work and in class.practice: “Although the old rooms are larger, we’ll book the new ones.” What is the decision?

Writing for an audience.title: Polite professional requests
Writing for an audience.instruction: Give brief context, one clear request and a useful time frame.
Writing for an audience.practice: Ask a colleague for the latest figures by Thursday.
Writing for an audience.answer: “Could you send me the latest figures by Thursday so I can update the slides?”

Writing for an audience.title: Paragraph links
Writing for an audience.instruction: Repeat a key term or use a connector that describes the relationship.
Writing for an audience.practice: Add a sentence that contrasts with “The room is affordable.”
Writing for an audience.answer: “However, it is too small for the whole group.”

Writing for an audience.title: Acknowledge a drawback
Writing for an audience.instruction: State a relevant objection before explaining why your decision still holds.
Writing for an audience.practice: Recommend hybrid meetings while noting a problem.
Writing for an audience.answer: “Although sound quality may vary, hybrid meetings let colleagues outside the city participate.”

Speaking in short turns.title: Point, reason, example
Speaking in short turns.instruction: Start with an answer, add a reason and finish with a concrete example.
Speaking in short turns.practice: Speak for 30 seconds on the best place to study.
Speaking in short turns.answer: “I prefer the library because it is quiet. I can read for an hour without interruptions.”

Speaking in short turns.title: Compare aloud
Speaking in short turns.instruction: Name one shared feature, one difference and a preference.
Speaking in short turns.practice: Compare an online workshop and a classroom workshop.
Speaking in short turns.answer: “Both teach the same topic, but the classroom workshop gives me more chances to ask questions.”

Speaking in short turns.title: Make yourself understood
Speaking in short turns.instruction: Pause between ideas and restate a word if you get stuck.

use-of-english.title: Use of English Placement
use-of-english.description: Find gaps in grammar and vocabulary and listen for meaning in everyday exchanges.

Verb forms in context.title: Completed past events
Verb forms in context.instruction: Use the past simple with a stated finished time.

Verb forms in context.title: Ongoing states
Verb forms in context.instruction: Use “since” for a starting point and “for” for a duration.
Verb forms in context.answer: “Since” introduces the year the situation began.

Verb forms in context.title: Real future conditions
Verb forms in context.instruction: Use present simple in a basic “if” clause about a possible future event.
Verb forms in context.practice: Complete “If the train ___ late, we’ll call.”
Verb forms in context.answer: “Is” is the usual form in this condition.

Vocabulary and meaning.title: Collocations
Vocabulary and meaning.instruction: Learn common word partnerships in a short example.

Vocabulary and meaning.title: Phrasal verbs
Vocabulary and meaning.instruction: Compare the meaning of a phrase in a complete sentence.
Vocabulary and meaning.practice: In “They put off the meeting until Monday,” what does “put off” mean?

Vocabulary and meaning.title: Context clues
Vocabulary and meaning.instruction: Use the consequences in a sentence to infer an unknown word.
Vocabulary and meaning.practice: In “The shop was deserted, so we could hear every footstep,” what does “deserted” suggest?
Vocabulary and meaning.answer: Very few people, or nobody, were there.

Everyday listening.title: Numbers and changes
Everyday listening.instruction: Record the first number and listen for a correction.
Everyday listening.practice: “Platform five, sorry, platform nine.” Which platform should you use?

Everyday listening.title: Indirect requests
Everyday listening.instruction: A question with “could” often asks someone to do something.
Everyday listening.practice: What response fits “Could you hold the door?”

Everyday listening.title: Attitude and reason
Everyday listening.instruction: Listen for phrases such as “I’m afraid” and “I’m pleased” and the reason that follows.
Everyday listening.practice: “I’d love to, but I’m working then.” Can the person join?
Everyday listening.answer: No. The person is working at that time.

Writing from a clear prompt.title: Read all task requirements
Writing from a clear prompt.instruction: Underline the audience, topic and number of points requested.
Writing from a clear prompt.practice: What must you provide for “Write to your tutor with two reasons for changing class”?
Writing from a clear prompt.answer: A message to the tutor and two reasons for the request.

Writing from a clear prompt.title: Develop a reason
Writing from a clear prompt.instruction: Explain the practical effect of each reason.
Writing from a clear prompt.practice: Develop “The later class is better for me.”
Writing from a clear prompt.answer: “It starts after my shift, so I can arrive on time.”

Writing from a clear prompt.title: Check familiar errors
Writing from a clear prompt.instruction: Read your verbs and time phrases together during revision.
Writing from a clear prompt.practice: Fix “Yesterday I have finished the report.”

integrated.title: Integrated English Placement
integrated.description: Interpret practical information and communicate it clearly in written and spoken responses.

Selecting source details.title: Read a notice
Selecting source details.instruction: Identify who is affected, what changes and when the change starts.
Selecting source details.practice: “From Monday, evening students enter through Gate B.” Who uses Gate B?

Selecting source details.title: Capture figures accurately
Selecting source details.instruction: Write numbers with units and note what they describe.
Selecting source details.practice: A speaker says “The room holds eighteen, although only twelve are registered.” What is the capacity?

Selecting source details.title: Separate fact and opinion
Selecting source details.instruction: Treat a measured or directly checkable detail differently from a judgement.
Selecting source details.practice: Which is checkable, “The course runs for six weeks” or “The course is excellent”?

Listening and reporting.title: Summarize an announcement
Listening and reporting.instruction: Write the action first and include an essential detail.
Listening and reporting.practice: A speaker moves orientation from upstairs to the lobby because the lift is broken. Summarize.
Listening and reporting.answer: “Orientation will take place in the lobby because the lift is broken.”

Listening and reporting.title: Compare spoken and written news
Listening and reporting.instruction: Use the latest dated source to confirm changes.
Listening and reporting.practice: An email sent Tuesday moves Friday’s workshop to Saturday, but an older poster says Friday. Which is current?
Listening and reporting.answer: Saturday, based on the newer email.

Listening and reporting.title: Retell without copying
Listening and reporting.instruction: Use shorter words where possible and keep names and facts accurate.
Listening and reporting.practice: Paraphrase “Participants must vacate the premises by six.”
Listening and reporting.answer: “Everyone taking part must leave the building by six.”

Practical writing.title: Subject lines
Practical writing.instruction: Name the action or event in a few words.
Practical writing.practice: Write a subject line for asking to extend Friday’s deadline.

Practical writing.title: Prioritize information
Practical writing.instruction: Place the action readers need first, then explain the reason.
Practical writing.practice: Write a first sentence about a cancelled room.
Practical writing.answer: “Please meet in Room 8 today because Room 5 is closed.”

Practical writing.title: Evidence in a recommendation
Practical writing.instruction: Use one source detail and show how it affects the choice.
Practical writing.practice: Why might a lab that stays open until eight suit working students?
Practical writing.answer: They have time to use the lab after their shifts.

Spoken responses.title: One-minute plan
Spoken responses.instruction: Jot down the main idea, two details and a closing line.
Spoken responses.practice: Give an order for a spoken update on a schedule change.
Spoken responses.answer: Start with the new date, explain the room and reason, then tell listeners how to confirm.

Spoken responses.title: Repair a mistake
Spoken responses.instruction: Use a brief correction and continue speaking.
Spoken responses.practice: You said Monday but meant Tuesday. Correct it aloud.
Spoken responses.answer: “Sorry, I mean Tuesday. We’ll meet at nine.”

Spoken responses.title: Stress essential contrasts
Spoken responses.instruction: Emphasize the changed part of a sentence.
Spoken responses.practice: In “Bring the form on Friday rather than Monday,” which two words should be stressed?

general.title: General English Placement
general.skills: Listening, grammar, vocabulary, reading and writing
general.description: Review a broad range of everyday English used in class and around campus.

Listening around campus.title: Identify a destination
Listening around campus.instruction: Listen for location words after verbs such as “go,” “turn,” and “meet.”
Listening around campus.practice: “Meet outside the office, across from the café.” Where should you wait?

Listening around campus.title: Listen for a reason
Listening around campus.practice: “The teacher took us inside because it was raining.” Why did they move?

Listening around campus.title: Follow a short exchange
Listening around campus.instruction: Keep one line of notes for each person’s plan.
Listening around campus.practice: One friend has a class at five. The other suggests meeting at six. When can they meet?

Grammar and vocabulary.title: Articles and sound
Grammar and vocabulary.instruction: Choose “a” or “an” according to the first sound.

Grammar and vocabulary.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
Grammar and vocabulary.instruction: Use “many” for plural countable nouns and “much” for uncountable nouns.

Grammar and vocabulary.title: Polite requests
Grammar and vocabulary.instruction: Use a modal with a base verb to make a polite request.
Grammar and vocabulary.practice: Change “Open the window” into a polite question.

Reading useful texts.title: Signs and rules
Reading useful texts.instruction: Look for the action a sign permits or prohibits.
Reading useful texts.practice: What does “Staff only beyond this point” mean?
Reading useful texts.answer: Only staff may continue past the sign.

Reading useful texts.title: Timetables
Reading useful texts.instruction: Check day, time and any exceptions in the notes.
Reading useful texts.practice: A class meets daily except Tuesday. Is it offered on Tuesday?

Reading useful texts.title: Simple inference
Reading useful texts.instruction: Combine two details that the writer gives you.
Reading useful texts.practice: The café is closed and Lina has no food with her. Why might she go to a shop?

Writing for study.title: Topic sentences
Writing for study.instruction: Introduce one main idea at the start of a paragraph.
Writing for study.practice: Write a topic sentence about a study routine.
Writing for study.answer: “Reviewing my notes each evening helps me remember new words.”

Writing for study.title: Examples from everyday life
Writing for study.instruction: Show your idea in a specific situation.
Writing for study.practice: Give an example of studying on a bus.
Writing for study.answer: “I review five vocabulary cards on my way to class.”

Writing for study.title: Revision in three passes
Writing for study.instruction: Check meaning first, then sentence boundaries, then spelling.
Writing for study.practice: Fix “I study at home my brother studies at the library.”
Writing for study.answer: “I study at home. My brother studies at the library.”

remote.title: Remote English Placement
remote.description: Work through short digital tasks and produce an extended response in your own words.

On-screen reading.title: Track reference words
On-screen reading.instruction: Connect “they,” “these,” and “this” to the idea they refer to.
On-screen reading.practice: “The articles cover three topics. They are available online.” What does “they” refer to?

On-screen reading.title: Read between sentences
On-screen reading.instruction: Use connectors to identify cause, contrast and example.
On-screen reading.practice: What connection does “therefore” mark in “The roads flooded. Therefore, the bus was cancelled”?
On-screen reading.answer: The cancellation is a result of the flooding.

On-screen reading.title: Choose an accurate summary
On-screen reading.instruction: Check that a summary contains the central point and avoids adding facts.
On-screen reading.practice: Summarize “The app saved time, but its reminders often arrived late.”
On-screen reading.answer: “The app helped users work faster despite unreliable reminders.”

Short listening tasks.title: Key words in a short message
Short listening tasks.instruction: Listen first for the main point. Check one missing detail on a replay if available.
Short listening tasks.practice: “The slides are ready, but wait until Wednesday to share them.” What action is delayed?

Short listening tasks.title: Stress and contrast
Short listening tasks.instruction: The stressed word often shows what the speaker is correcting.
Short listening tasks.practice: In “I said the green folder,” the word “green” is stressed. What is being clarified?
Short listening tasks.answer: Which colour of folder is meant.

Short listening tasks.title: Reconstruct a message
Short listening tasks.instruction: Keep the time, location and required action in your notes.
Short listening tasks.practice: “At ten, take your ID to the main hall.” Retell it.
Short listening tasks.answer: “Go to the main hall at ten with your ID.”

Writing under a deadline.title: Plan with two ideas
Writing under a deadline.instruction: Spend a few minutes choosing two distinct reasons and one example for each.
Writing under a deadline.practice: Give two different reasons for using digital textbooks.
Writing under a deadline.answer: They are lighter to carry, and search makes definitions easier to find.

Writing under a deadline.title: Connect sentences
Writing under a deadline.instruction: Link an example or consequence to the point that it supports.
Writing under a deadline.practice: After “Short videos are convenient,” add a consequence.
Writing under a deadline.answer: “As a result, students can review a lesson during a short break.”

Writing under a deadline.title: Final edit
Writing under a deadline.instruction: Check the prompt, verb agreement and missing words before returning your work.
Writing under a deadline.practice: Fix “One of the benefits are flexibility.”

Speaking remotely.title: Check your microphone
Speaking remotely.instruction: Make a short recording in a quiet place and listen at normal volume.
Speaking remotely.practice: What should you check in a ten-second test?
Speaking remotely.answer: That the voice is clear and background sound is low.

Speaking remotely.title: Describe a scene
Speaking remotely.instruction: Start with the main action and add details you can directly observe.
Speaking remotely.practice: Describe a scene with two students and a map.
Speaking remotely.answer: “Two students are looking at an open map. One is pointing to a route.”

Speaking remotely.title: Support an opinion aloud
Speaking remotely.instruction: State a position and add one practical example.
Speaking remotely.practice: Should schools offer online office hours? Give one reason and an example.
Speaking remotely.answer: “Yes. It helps students who live far away. For example, they can ask about an assignment without travelling to campus.”
